Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a comparison of two approaches to background jobs: a queue with workers, and scheduled batch runs. Around 200 words.

A queue with workers fits jobs that arrive unpredictably and need to run soon after they're created: image resizing, email sends, webhook delivery. Producers push a task, a pool of workers pulls from the queue, and idle capacity sits ready. Throughput scales by adding workers, and each task fails or retries on its own without affecting the others.

Scheduled batch runs fit jobs tied to a clock instead of an event: nightly reports, daily reconciliation, hourly cache rebuilds. A cron trigger starts the job, it processes a full set of records, and it exits. There's no persistent worker pool to manage, and a single run is easy to reason about and debug, but a burst of new records between runs waits for the next scheduled slot.

The real tradeoff is latency versus operational weight. A queue delivers near-real-time processing but needs monitoring for stuck workers, dead-letter handling, and backpressure when producers outrun consumers. A batch job accepts delay in exchange for a simpler failure mode: rerun the job. Systems with steady, bursty, latency-sensitive traffic lean toward queues; systems with periodic, bulk, deadline-driven work lean toward batch. Many production systems use both — a queue for user-facing events, a nightly batch for aggregation and cleanup that doesn't need to happen the moment data lands.

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a paragraph on what happens when a job fails in each.

In a queue, one job's failure is isolated. It retries a fixed number of times with backoff, then lands in a dead-letter queue for inspection while the rest of the workers keep pulling from the main queue. The system needs a place to look at those dead-lettered jobs and a way to replay them once the cause is fixed, or failures accumulate unseen.

In a batch run, a failure partway through leaves the question of what already committed. A job that isn't idempotent can double-process the records it got through before crashing, so the safe version tracks a checkpoint or processes records in a transaction per batch, and a full rerun either skips completed work or safely repeats it. Without that design, the fix is "run it again" but with no guarantee about what state the partial run left behind.

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a recommendation for a small team.

A queue suits a small team when jobs are user-facing and delay is visible: a signup email, a webhook. A batch job suits internal work with a natural daily or hourly rhythm: a report, a cleanup pass. A small team should default to batch first. It runs on the same cron infrastructure they likely already have, needs no separate worker fleet, and a stuck job is just a log to read the next morning. Add a queue only when a specific job needs to run within seconds of being created, and even then, one small worker pool with a dead-letter queue and an alert on its depth covers most needs. Running both a queue and a complex batch pipeline before either is required adds two operational surfaces for a team that can staff one.
